conventions.convention: Stability predicates quantify over maximal solutions whose intervals contain 0, require existence for all nonnegative times, and do not assert existence or uniqueness for an arbitrary right-hand side.
Orbital stability concerns distance to a nonempty forward-invariant set; linear stability means boundedness of every maximal solution of the linearized system on [0,∞).

Hyperbolicity tests the complex-linear extension: continuous-time eigenvalues avoid real part zero, while map eigenvalues avoid modulus one. Periodic orbits are images of nonconstant globally periodic solutions; isolation, rather than attraction, defines a limit cycle.
The stroboscopic map uses initial time 0 and P>0, with domain D_P consisting precisely of states whose maximal interval contains [0,P]. Each successive iterate requires another membership in D_P.
All particle masses are strictly positive. Configuration dimension d may be zero; X is a smooth map and need not be an immersion. The mass metric is its pullback of the block-weighted Euclidean form.

A material region is nonempty, bounded and open, with no boundary regularity built in. Lebesgue density and mass assume Countable Choice; densities are nonnegative measurable integrable functions and need not be strictly positive or continuous.

t(n) is force per area exerted by material toward which n points upon material on the opposite side. Representation means t(n)=σn for every unit n; neither representation nor t(-n)=-t(n) is assumed for an arbitrary traction.

The time functional τ is fixed, surjective and unscaled. The spatial inner product exists only on K=ker τ. Adapted spatial bases are positively oriented for one fixed orientation of K; distances are defined only within simultaneous slices.
SO(3) consists of real matrices satisfying RᵀR=I and det R=1, with the Euclidean topology inherited from matrix-entry coordinates.
Moving-frame angular velocity uses the body convention Ω=RᵀR′ and Ωz=ω×z, with the right-handed cross product. The acceleration identity assumes C2 curves on a nondegenerate interval.
The stabilizer fixes each label individually; it is a pointwise stabilizer, not a setwise stabilizer. Two independent vectors suffice without requiring the origin as a label.
The spherical coordinate domain is (0,π)×(0,2π), excluding both poles and the positive-x longitude seam. Coordinate degeneration at poles does not imply degeneration of the intrinsic mass metric.

load_bearing.statement: V has real dimension 4; τ:V→R is surjective linear; K=ker τ carries an inner product and fixed orientation; A is a nonempty affine space modelled on V. An adapted chart consists of o∈A, τ(u)=1 and a positively oriented orthonormal basis of K.

Every event has unique adapted coordinates, the coordinate map is bijective, simultaneous slices are affine spaces over K with Euclidean coordinate distance, and an adapted chart exists for every admissible set of data and fixed orientation.

Two adapted charts satisfy t′=t+b and x′=Rx+vt+a, with R∈O(3) and R∈SO(3) under their positive-orientation convention. Time-parametrized C1/C2 coordinate curves satisfy y′=Rx′+v and y″=Rx″; zero acceleration is preserved in both directions.

An equilibrium satisfies F(z*)=0. Lyapunov stability requires that every sufficiently close maximal solution exists for all t≥0 and remains within each admissible test radius; asymptotic stability additionally requires convergence for all sufficiently close maximal solutions.

For C2 R:I→SO(3), c:I→R³ and y:I→R³ on a nondegenerate interval, Ω=RᵀR′ is skew and has a unique C1 representative ω with Ωz=ω×z. If x=Ry+c, then Rᵀx″=y″+2ω×y′+ω′×y+ω×(ω×y)+Rᵀc″. Rotations preserve Euclidean norms.
For smooth X:Q→R^(3N) and positive masses, G_q(u,v)=⟨dX_q(u),M dX_q(v)⟩, and T_q(v)=G_q(v,v)/2.
G_q is symmetric bilinear and positive semidefinite; it is positive definite if and only if dX_q is injective. Its matrix in a tangent basis is AᵀMA.
SO(3) contains I₃ and is closed under products and transposes; R is invertible with inverse Rᵀ. Consequently SO(3) is a subgroup of GL₃(R).
SO(3) is a three-dimensional embedded submanifold of M₃(R), open and closed in O(3), with T_R SO(3)={RΩ:Ωᵀ=-Ω}; it is compact.
For continuous, locally state-Lipschitz, P-periodic F:R×U→Rⁿ with U open and P>0, θ_P:D_P→U is θ_P(z)=x_z(P), where D_P={z∈U:[0,P]⊆J_z}.
If z∈D_P and θ_P(z)∈D_P, then [0,2P]⊆J_z and θ_P(θ_P(z))=x_z(2P). If F(t,z*)=0 for every real t, then z*∈D_P and θ_P(z*)=z*.
Let u,v∈R³ be linearly independent and S⊆R³ contain them. If R∈SO(3) fixes every s∈S, then R=I₃; equivalently its pointwise stabilizer is {I₃}.

concerns.concern: F5 attributes to prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure the additional conclusions 'embedded in the ambient manifold' and 'its tangent space ... is the ambient tangent space there'. The cited Statement establishes the restricted smooth structure but does not state these additional conclusions. Step 4.1 uses both to transfer embeddedness and the tangent formula from O(3) to SO(3). Restricted slice charts and the identity coordinate representation of the open inclusion close this short gap, but that argument is omitted.

alerts.finding: Verification 1.3 says zero coordinate acceleration 'is preserved by every Galilean change of frame by clause 1 of lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations'. Clause 1 supplies the affine coordinate transformation; clause 2 supplies its derivative laws and clause 3 explicitly supplies the zero-acceleration iff. The mathematical conclusion is correct, but the clause locator is incorrect.

seams_checked.note: Affine data, oriented adapted charts, configuration mass metric and Galilean derivative laws retain their supplier scope; physical adoption is explicit.
Boost, rod configuration and rotating-basis checks use the corresponding coordinate, mass-metric and C2 acceleration formulas.
Rotation inverse and inner-product identities are used with R∈SO(3); cross-product covariance has separate mathematical support.
Stability uses maximal forward solutions. The strict-minimum consumer distinguishes unrestricted autonomous extensions from the declared model time window.
Moving charts are C2 and use Ω=RᵀR′; the full acceleration identity and Galilean frame law are restated faithfully.
The explicit rotating chart uses the same body angular velocity, norm preservation and acceleration terms.
The fixed-axis rotation is explicitly computed and verified as SO(3)-valued; no stronger manifold or dynamical conclusion is attributed to the geometry suppliers.
Lyapunov stability and instability retain maximal-solution and all-forward-time meanings; linear versus nonlinear conclusions remain distinguished.
The unstable quadratic example uses a fixed escape radius and separately states the hypotheses for nonlinear instability.
SO(3) dimension, topology and group facts are preserved. Pointwise labeling faithfulness retains the two-independent-vector hypothesis and accounts separately for translation.
Examples distinguish Euler-coordinate degeneracy from the rotation itself and use ordinary SO(3) algebra.
Body rotation conventions and maximal-solution definitions of linear and Lyapunov stability are preserved; orientation closeness is expressly excluded from angular-momentum stability.
The control-volume model adds boundary regularity, positive C1 density and represented traction; Countable Choice is explicit.
The stability definition repeats the supplier quantifiers and global forward-existence requirement; spectral and nonlinear conclusions require separate results.
Region, density and traction conventions are preserved. Stronger field regularity and positivity belong to the declared physical branch; Lebesgue mass carries Countable Choice.
The traction counterexample correctly treats reversed-normal symmetry as insufficient for matrix representation.
Local-flow terminology distinguishes the partial stroboscopic map; stability results require and establish maximal forward existence.
The nonhyperbolic counterexample uses the maximal-solution stability predicate without asserting exponential decay from stability alone.
Material regions receive additional motion and boundary hypotheses. Stress representation and symmetry are conditional results, and row divergence matches t(n)=σn.
The translating-flow example uses a nonempty bounded open ball as its material region.
Rotation inverse and cross-product conventions agree; C1 rotation calculus is proved locally rather than attributed to the C2 acceleration lemma.
The periodic pulse system is smooth and state-Lipschitz; its endpoint-map identification retains the stroboscopic existence domain.
The C1 body-angular-velocity result supplies its own proof and explicitly restricts comparison with the acceleration supplier to C2 paths.
The affine arena and positively oriented adapted frames retain the time and spatial conventions; a local construction establishes the converse realization of every Galilean parameter quadruple.
The quadratic-shear conclusion is mathematically consistent, but Verification 1.3 cites clause 1 for zero-acceleration preservation, which is explicitly clause 3. Routed as a presentation alert.
Spatial rotations use the Euclidean SO(3) topology, inverse transpose and determinant one; operator-domain and measure claims have separate suppliers.
The radial-potential example uses norm preservation and determinant-one substitution, with null-set and operator conclusions separately justified.
The SU(2) lift uses SO(3) as defined and explicitly transports the covering map by the stated axis rotation C.
Sphere rotations use SO(3) group laws, Euclidean matrix topology and inverse transpose; operator and Frobenius norms are explicitly distinguished.
